newsitem.title: USA: GM, UAW reach deal to end strike at Indiana plant.
newsitem.headline: GM, UAW reach deal to end strike at Indiana plant.

text.p: General Motors Corp. said Thursday it reached a tentative agreement with the United Auto Workers union to end a nearly two-week strike at the automaker's Fort Wayne, Ind., pickup truck plant.

The strike reduced GM's production of the popular Chevrolet C/K and GMC Sierra full-size pickups, but did not cause widespread shortages in dealer showrooms. GM produces the trucks at three other plants, in Pontiac and Flint, Mich., and Oshawa, Ontario.
The full-size trucks are among GM's most profitable vehicles, and Wall Street analysts estimated that the lost output will reduce the automaker's first quarter earnings by $40 million to $50 million.

The deal, which union officials said calls for GM to hire up to 300 new workers at the plant, was scheduled for a ratification vote by members of UAW Local 2209 at 8 p.m. Thursday. The accord was reached early Thursday morning.

"If the agreement is ratified by the work force, employees will return to work at their regular shift starting times on Tuesday, April 1," said Thomas Beaman, a spokesman for the GM Truck Group in Pontiac, Mich.
GM declined to comment on the terms of the agreement.
None of GM's U.S. plants were scheduled to operate on Friday and Monday because of the Easter holiday weekend.

The UAW struck the Fort Wayne facility on March 14 when negotiations failed to produce a new local labor contract for the plant. The major sticking point was manpower levels at the factory, which employs about 2,700 UAW members.
"This plant's always in constant turnover of its workforce. Somewhere along the line, more workers flowed out than flowed in," said Charlie Gamble, a spokesman for Local 2209.
Many of GM's plants are experiencing record rates of retirements, and the automaker is aiming to improve its efficiency by limiting the amount of new workers it hires to replace them.

Lehman Brothers auto analyst Joseph Phillippi said significant new hiring at GM's truck plants could leave the automaker with excess workers once it launches production of its next-generation full-size pickup trucks in late 1998.
The so-called GMT-800 trucks will require about 30 percent fewer labor hours to produce, he said.

The staffing issue has caused problems with local negotiations at nearly every GM plant in the United States. On Wednesday, UAW Local 1999 in Oklahoma City notified GM that it would strike on April 4 if no local pact was reached by then.
A strike in Oklahoma would largely cut off supplies of GM's critical new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass mid-size cars just as they are starting to appear in national advertising campaigns.
Bear Stearns & Co. analyst Nicholas Lobocarro said the Fort Wayne strike cost GM about $40 million, or 5 cents a share, based on production of about 1,000 trucks a day.
Phillippi pegged the strike's first quarter cost at $50 million, or about 7 cents a share, but added that GM can probably make up the lost production during the second quarter.
"Fortunately, these were the plain-vanilla, regular cab trucks that they lost, not the loaded, extended cab trucks," Phillippi said.
